caption:
10 Must-Know Time Complexity Patterns for Interviews

1. 𝐇𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐋𝐨𝐨𝐤𝐮𝐩 - 𝐎(1) 𝐚𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞
A lookup usually takes constant time, regardless of input size. In the worst case, it can degrade to O(n).

2. 𝐇𝐚𝐥𝐯𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐋𝐨𝐨𝐩 - 𝐎(𝐥𝐨𝐠 𝐧)
The input size is divided by a constant factor in every step, such as in binary search.

3. 𝐒𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐥𝐞 𝐋𝐨𝐨𝐩 - 𝐎(𝐧)
Each element is processed once.

4. 𝐒𝐞𝐪𝐮𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐋𝐨𝐨𝐩𝐬 - 𝐎(𝐧 + 𝐦)
You iterate over two separate inputs one after another, not with one loop nested inside the other.

5. 𝐋𝐨𝐨𝐩 + 𝐁𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐫𝐲 𝐒𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐜𝐡 - 𝐎(𝐧 𝐥𝐨𝐠 𝐧)
A loop runs n times, and each iteration performs O(log n) work.

6. 𝐃𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐝𝐞 & 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐪𝐮𝐞𝐫 - 𝐎(𝐧 𝐥𝐨𝐠 𝐧)
The problem is divided across roughly log n levels, with O(n) total work at each level. Merge sort is a common example.

7. 𝐍𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐋𝐨𝐨𝐩𝐬 - 𝐎(𝐧²)
For every element, you iterate over all elements again.

8. 𝐓𝐫𝐢𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐮𝐥𝐚𝐫 𝐋𝐨𝐨𝐩 - 𝐎(𝐧²)
The inner loop performs fewer iterations each time, but the total is still roughly n(n − 1) / 2, which is quadratic.

9. 𝐁𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐑𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧 - 𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐨𝐧𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐓𝐢𝐦𝐞
When each recursive call creates multiple new calls, the work can grow exponentially.

10. 𝐏𝐞𝐫𝐦𝐮𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 - 𝐎(𝐧!)
There are n! possible orderings, and producing or copying each complete permutation can take O(n) time.

Liquid Al, the MIT spinout, just released Antidoom. 

It exists to fix one of Al’s biggest flaws! Antidoom targets the exact token score that triggers repetitive “doom loops” - the glitch that wastes context windows and ruins Al reasoning. 

It’s fully open source; and any developer can use it to unlock significantly more power. That said, using it requires serious hardware and deep Al knowledge.

This video will help you build that Knowledge!

#learnai #ainews #learnoninstagram #opensource #gigaqian
transcript: Antidoom is so useful, but the name is a bit spooky, so I'll explain what it is, and by the end of this video, you'll understand how to make your favorite AI models so much smarter without teaching them anything. I'm Giga Chan, and I want you to be successful, so I'm going to make some complicated concepts easy to understand, so ask me if you have questions. Liquid AI is an MIT spin-out building efficient AI, and I mean efficient. One of their models can run entirely offline on your phone, using less than 900 megabytes of memory. Antidoom is not a model, it's an open-source training pipeline for fixing existing models, and it's cooler than it sounds. If you give AI a hard problem and watch it think, you might see things like, wait, let me reconsider. Then you might watch it repeat itself until it uses up its context window. That's the limited amount of text it can reference at once. And some of us call that failure a doom loop. Aha. AI generates one token, which is essentially a word or a part of a word, at a time. Antidoom scans the text to find where a long phrase starts repeating, and then it targets the exact token that restarts the doom loop. That token becomes the rejected choice. Sorry, little guy. Antidoom then looks at the model's data and picks up to 20 alternatives. These are the chosen tokens. This is called Final Token Preference Optimization, FTPO if you want to sound like an expert. It trains to prefer those alternatives at that exact situation. Suppressing one token too aggressively could damage reasoning, so FTPO uses a KL-like regularizer. Don't let that scare you. KL stands for Callback-Liebler Divergence. It's just a way to measure how different one probability distribution is from another. An irregularizer is a penalty. It's meant to discourage the model from changing more than is necessary. Pay attention because this is the part of the video that will level most of you up. This penalty works in logit space. Preference are the model's raw scores for every possible next token before the scores become probabilities. Okay, take a breath. We're done with that. You can ask me more technicals in the comments, but the point is Antidoom eliminated the vast majority of doom loops across the models it was tested on, up to over 95%. These are company-reported results on smaller models, so it doesn't necessarily mean you can let this thing run rampant on Claude or GPT.
